nodes.name: Assignment vector
nodes.statement: For each patient m ge 1, the assignment vector X_m = (X_m,1, dots, X_m,K) takes values in \0,1\^K and satisfies sum_k=1^K X_m,k = 1. The event \X_m,k = 1\ means that patient m is assigned to arm k.

nodes.name: Responses and parameters
nodes.statement: For each arm k in [K], \xi_m,k : m ge 1\ is a sequence of i.i.d.\ real random variables, the potential responses of patients on treatment k. The parameter of interest for arm k is the mean theta_k := E[xi_1,k], and Theta = (theta_1, dots, theta_K) in R^K. We write V_k := Var[xi_1,k] for the variance of the response of arm k.
nodes.raw_latex:
\label{def:responses}
For each arm $k \in [K]$, $\{\xi_{m,k} : m \ge 1\}$ is a sequence of i.i.d.\
real random variables, the potential responses of patients on treatment $k$.
The parameter of interest for arm $k$ is the mean
$\theta_k := \mathbb{E}[\xi_{1,k}]$, and $\Theta = (\theta_1, \dots, \theta_K) \in \mathbb{R}^K$.
We write $V_k := \mathbb{V}\mathrm{ar}[\xi_{1,k}]$ for the variance of the response of arm $k$.

nodes.name: RAR procedure
nodes.statement: A response-adaptive randomization (RAR) procedure is a sequence (p_m)_m ge 1 of F_m-measurable random vectors taking values in the probability simplex \[ Delta_K := Big\ p in [0,1]^K : sum_k=1^K p_k = 1 Big\, \] such that the assignment X_m+1 is drawn conditionally on F_m according to p_m: \[ P(X_m+1 = k mid F_m) = p_m,k, k in [K]. \]
nodes.raw_latex:
\label{def:rar}

A \emph{response-adaptive randomization (RAR) procedure} is a sequence
$(p_m)_{m \ge 1}$ of $\mathcal{F}_m$-measurable random vectors taking values in the
probability simplex
\[
  \Delta_K := \Big\{ p \in [0,1]^K : \sum_{k=1}^K p_k = 1 \Big\},
\]
such that the assignment $X_{m+1}$ is drawn conditionally on $\mathcal{F}_m$ according
to $p_m$:
\[
  \mathbb{P}(X_{m+1} = k \mid \mathcal{F}_m) = p_{m,k}, \qquad k \in [K].
\]

nodes.label: def:rar

nodes.name: Target function and target allocation
nodes.statement: A target function is a map rho : H to Delta_K defined on an open domain H subseteq R^K, written rho(z) = (rho_1(z), dots, rho_K(z)) with sum_k=1^K rho_k(z) = 1. The target allocation is v := rho(Theta). A RAR procedure is an adaptive targeting mechanism if N_n/n to v.
nodes.raw_latex:
\label{def:target}
A \emph{target function} is a map $\rho : \mathcal{H} \to \Delta_K$ defined on an
open domain $\mathcal{H} \subseteq \mathbb{R}^K$, written
$\rho(z) = (\rho_1(z), \dots, \rho_K(z))$ with
$\sum_{k=1}^K \rho_k(z) = 1$. The \emph{target allocation} is
$v := \rho(\Theta)$. A RAR procedure is an \emph{adaptive targeting
mechanism} if $N_n/n \to v$.

nodes.name: Sequential estimator
nodes.statement: Given initial values theta_0,k in R, the sequential estimator of theta_k at stage m is \[ hattheta_m,k := fracsum_j=1^m X_j,k\, xi_j,k + theta_0,kN_m,k + 1. \] We write hatTheta_m := (hattheta_m,1, dots, hattheta_m,K).
nodes.raw_latex:
\label{def:estimator}


Given initial values $\theta_{0,k} \in \mathbb{R}$, the sequential estimator of
$\theta_k$ at stage $m$ is
\[
  \hat{\theta}_{m,k} := \frac{\sum_{j=1}^m X_{j,k}\, \xi_{j,k} + \theta_{0,k}}{N_{m,k} + 1}.
\]
We write $\hat{\Theta}_m := (\hat{\theta}_{m,1}, \dots, \hat{\theta}_{m,K})$.

nodes.name: Bahadur representation
nodes.statement: An estimator hattheta_m,k of theta_k admits a Bahadur representation if \[ hattheta_m,k = frac1N_m,ksum_j=1^m X_j,k\, xi_j,k + o\!big(N_m,k^-1/2big), m to infty. \]

\label{def:bahadur}

An estimator $\hat{\theta}_{m,k}$ of $\theta_k$ admits a \emph{Bahadur

    + o\!\big(N_{m,k}^{-1/2}\big), \qquad m \to \infty.
\]

nodes.raw_latex:
\label{lem:estimator_bahadur}


On the event $\{N_{m,k} \to \infty\}$, the estimator of
Definition~\ref{def:estimator} admits the Bahadur representation of
Definition~\ref{def:bahadur}. The formalized statement \texttt{estimator\_sub\_eq} is the sharper
\emph{exact} error identity
\[
  \hat{\theta}_{m,k} - \theta_k = \frac{Q_{m,k} + (\theta_{0,k} - \theta_k)}{N_{m,k} + 1},
\]
which holds pathwise for every $m$ (with $N_{m,k}+1 \ne 0$, automatic for $\{0,1\}$-indicators) and
from which the $o(N^{-1/2})$ Bahadur form is immediate.

nodes.name: $\alpha\text{RTS}$ family
nodes.statement: Let K ge 2, alpha in [0,1) and m_0 in N (a burn-in parameter). A RAR procedure is an alpha-Rebalancing Targeting Strategy (alphaRTS) if its allocation probabilities p_m+1 in Delta_K satisfy, for all m ge K m_0, the throttling condition forall k in [K], fracN_m,km > hatrho_m,k \ Longrightarrow\ p_m+1,k le alpha\, hatrho_m,k. In words: whenever arm k is currently over-sampled relative to its estimated target, the probability of selecting it next is throttled down to at most alpha hatrho_m,k.

In words: whenever arm k is currently over-sampled relative to its estimated target, the probability of selecting it next is throttled down to at most alpha hatrho_m,k.

nodes.raw_latex:
\label{def:distance_design}


Given $\alpha \in [0,1)$, the \emph{distance-based} design sets, for
$m \ge K m_0$ and $k \in [K]$,
\[
  p_{m+1,k} = \alpha\, \hat{\rho}_{m,k}

nodes.name: ERADE 2025 design
nodes.statement: Given alpha in [0,1), the ERADE 2025 design of sets, for m ge K m_0 and k in [K], \[ p_m+1,k = alpha hatrho_m,k, & N_m,k/m > hatrho_m,k,\\ hatrho_m,k, & N_m,k/m = hatrho_m,k,\\ hatrho_m,k + (1-alpha)dfracsum_jin Shatrho_m,j|T|, & N_m,k/m < hatrho_m,k, \] where S = \ j : N_m,j/m > hatrho_m,j\ is the set of over-sampled arms and T = \ j : N_m,j/m < hatrho_m,j\ the set of under-sampled arms.
nodes.raw_latex:
\label{def:erade2025}


Given $\alpha \in [0,1)$, the \emph{ERADE 2025} design of
\cite{alkhnefr2025efficient} sets, for $m \ge K m_0$ and $k \in [K]$,
\[
  p_{m+1,k} =
  \begin{cases}
    \alpha \hat{\rho}_{m,k}, & N_{m,k}/m > \hat{\rho}_{m,k},\\
    \hat{\rho}_{m,k}, & N_{m,k}/m = \hat{\rho}_{m,k},\\
    \hat{\rho}_{m,k} + (1-\alpha)\dfrac{\sum_{j\in S}\hat{\rho}_{m,j}}{|T|},
      & N_{m,k}/m < \hat{\rho}_{m,k},
  \end{cases}
\]
where $S = \{ j : N_{m,j}/m > \hat{\rho}_{m,j}\}$ is the set of over-sampled arms
and $T = \{ j : N_{m,j}/m < \hat{\rho}_{m,j}\}$ the set of under-sampled arms.

nodes.raw_latex:
\label{def:d_tracking}


For $\alpha \in [0,1)$, the \emph{Interpolated D-Tracking} rule sets, for
$m \ge K m_0$ and $k \in [K]$,
\[
  p_{m+1,k} = \alpha\, \hat{\rho}_{m,k} + (1-\alpha)\,\mathbf{1}_{\{k = k^\star\}},
  \qquad
  k^\star \in arg\,max_{a \in [K]} \big\{ m\hat{\rho}_{m,a} - N_{m,a} \big\}.
\]
The quantity $m\hat{\rho}_{m,a} - N_{m,a}$ is the deficit of arm $a$ relative to
its target, so $k^\star$ is the most under-sampled arm.

(\texttt{filtrationAction}): the assignment $X_{n,k}$ is $\mathcal{G}_n$-measurable
(the arm is known) while the response $\xi_{n,k}$ is not (it is revealed afterwards).

independently of the past given the arm, so its conditional mean is $\theta_k$;

$\mathbb{E}[\Delta Q_{n,k}\mid\mathcal{G}_n] = X_{n,k}(\theta_k-\theta_k)=0$, so $Q_{\cdot,k}$ is
a $\mathcal{G}$-martingale. Since $Q_{n,k}$ is $\mathcal{F}_{n-1}\subseteq\mathcal{G}_n$-measurable,

environment with per-arm reward kernel $\nu$, and $\theta_k = \int x\,\nu_k(dx)$ is
the kernel mean. The conditional-mean computation is \texttt{condExp\_feedback}
(which handles the first patient and the general step via the two conditional-distribution
fields of the framework), and the filtration $\mathcal{G}$ is \texttt{filtrationAction}.

$\mathbb{P}(\max_k |S_k| \ge x) \le \mathbb{E}[S_L^2]/x^2$. Orthogonality of martingale
increments yields $\mathbb{E}[S_L^2] = \sum_{k=1}^L \mathbb{E}|\Delta M_{n-L+k}|^2 \le L C_0$.
Combining, $\mathbb{P}(\max_m |M_n - M_{n-m}| \ge x) \le 4 L C_0 / x^2$, and integrating
the tail,
$\mathbb{E}[\max_m |M_n-M_{n-m}|] \le \int_0^{2\sqrt{LC_0}} 1\,dx
 + 4\int_{2\sqrt{LC_0}}^\infty \frac{LC_0}{x^2}\,dx = 4\sqrt{LC_0}$.

\label{prop:exp_fam}
For a regular one-parameter exponential family with density
$f(y\mid\eta) = \exp\{\eta y - A(\eta)\}h(y)$, if the parameter of interest
$\theta_k = A'(\eta_k)$ is the mean parameter and $\xi_{1,k} = Y$, then
$\mathbb{V}\mathrm{ar}(\xi_{1,k}) = I_k(\theta_k)^{-1}$, where $I_k$ is the Fisher information for
one observation.

nodes.statement: For the natural family, E_eta[Y] = A'(eta) and Var_eta(Y) = A''(eta). With theta_k = A'(eta_k) one has Var(xi_1,k) = A''(eta_k). By the reparameterization formula for Fisher information, I_k(theta_k) = I_eta_k(eta_k)big(fracdeta_kdtheta_kbig)^2 = A''(eta_k)big(frac1A''(eta_k)big)^2 = frac1A''(eta_k), so Var(xi_1,k) = I_k(theta_k)^-1.

For the natural family, $\mathbb{E}_\eta[Y] = A'(\eta)$ and $\mathbb{V}\mathrm{ar}_\eta(Y) = A''(\eta)$.
With $\theta_k = A'(\eta_k)$ one has $\mathbb{V}\mathrm{ar}(\xi_{1,k}) = A''(\eta_k)$. By the
reparameterization formula for Fisher information,
$I_k(\theta_k) = I_{\eta_k}(\eta_k)\big(\frac{d\eta_k}{d\theta_k}\big)^2
 = A''(\eta_k)\big(\frac{1}{A''(\eta_k)}\big)^2 = \frac{1}{A''(\eta_k)}$,

nodes.name: $\alpha\text{RTS}$ algorithm
nodes.statement: An algorithm chooses the action of patient n from a history h of the n completed rounds (patients 0,dots,n-1) via a Markov kernel; the probability it assigns to arm k is policy_n(h)(\k\). The algorithm is an alpha-throttled alphaRTS design with offsets Theta_0 and target map rho if its policy throttles every over-sampled arm: for every history h and arm k, if N_n,k(h) > n\,hatrho_k(h) then policy_n(h)(\k\) le alpha\,hatrho_k(h), where the count N(h) and target hatrho(h)=rho(hatTheta(h)) are computed from h. At n=0 the condition is vacuous, since N_0,k=0.
nodes.raw_latex:
\label{def:aRTS_alg}


An algorithm chooses the action of patient $n$ from a history $h$ of the $n$ completed rounds
(patients $0,\dots,n-1$) via a Markov kernel; the probability it assigns to arm $k$ is
$\mathrm{policy}_n(h)(\{k\})$. The algorithm
is an \emph{$\alpha$-throttled $\alpha\text{RTS}$ design} with offsets $\Theta_0$ and target map $\rho$ if
its policy throttles every over-sampled arm: for every history $h$ and arm $k$, if
$N_{n,k}(h) > n\,\hat\rho_k(h)$ then $\mathrm{policy}_n(h)(\{k\}) \le \alpha\,\hat\rho_k(h)$,
where the count $N(h)$ and target $\hat\rho(h)=\rho(\hat{\Theta}(h))$ are computed from $h$.
At $n=0$ the condition is vacuous, since $N_{0,k}=0$.

nodes.statement: The response martingale Q_cdot,k has predictable quadratic variation langle Q_krangle_n = V_k N_n,k (Lemma~). If V_k>0, then on \N_n,ktoinfty\ the bracket langle Q_krangle_n = V_k N_n,ktoinfty, so the bracket-normalized strong law (Theorem~) gives Q_n,k/langle Q_krangle_nto0, whence Q_n,k/N_n,k = V_k\,(Q_n,k/langle Q_krangle_n)to0. nodes.raw_latex:
The response martingale $Q_{\cdot,k}$ has predictable quadratic variation
$\langle Q_k\rangle_n = V_k N_{n,k}$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:Q_quad_var}). If $V_k>0$, then on
$\{N_{n,k}\to\infty\}$ the bracket $\langle Q_k\rangle_n = V_k N_{n,k}\to\infty$, so the
bracket-normalized strong law (Theorem~\ref{thm:mart_slln_bracket}) gives
$Q_{n,k}/\langle Q_k\rangle_n\to0$, whence
$Q_{n,k}/N_{n,k} = V_k\,(Q_{n,k}/\langle Q_k\rangle_n)\to0$. If $V_k=0$, then
$\mathbb{E}[Q_{n,k}^2] = V_k\,\mathbb{E}[N_{n,k}] = 0$, so $Q_{n,k}=0$ a.s.\ for every $n$ and the ratio is
identically $0$.

If V_k=0, then E[Q_n,k^2] = V_k\,E[N_n,k] = 0, so Q_n,k=0 a.s.\ for every n and the ratio is identically 0.

$\hat\theta_{n,k}-\theta_k = (Q_{n,k}+(\theta_{0,k}-\theta_k))/(N_{n,k}+1)$. On

A first-order Taylor expansion of $\rho$ around $\Theta$ (twice
differentiable by Condition~\textbf{B}) gives
$\hat{\rho}_n - v = G(\hat{\Theta}_n-\Theta) + O(\|\hat{\Theta}_n-\Theta\|^2)$
with $G := \nabla\rho|_\Theta$. Both terms are
$O(\sqrt{\log\log n / n})$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:theta_LIL}.

\emph{Formalization.} The delta-method core is formalized as \texttt{AlphaRAR.rho\_rate}: for a target
map $\rho$ merely \emph{differentiable} at $\Theta$ (the first-order part of Condition~\textbf{B};
the second-order term is unnecessary for the $O$-rate), if the estimator vector converges,
$\hat{\Theta}_n\to\Theta$ a.s.\ (Lemma~\ref{lem:theta_consistent}), with each coordinate at the rate
$\hat\theta_{n,k}-\theta_k = O(r_n)$ a.s.\ (Lemma~\ref{lem:theta_LIL}, $r_n=\sqrt{\log\log n/n}$),
then every coordinate of the plug-in target satisfies $\hat\rho_{n,k}-v_k = O(r_n)$ a.s. The
mechanism is the generic estimate \texttt{AlphaRAR.isBigO\_target\_sub\_of\_tendsto}: a differentiable
map sends $\hat{\Theta}_n-\Theta$ to $\rho(\hat{\Theta}_n)-\rho(\Theta)$ of the same big-$O$ order
(\texttt{AlphaRAR.isBigO\_sub\_comp\_of\_differentiableAt}, from \texttt{HasFDerivAt.isBigO\_sub}),
combined coordinatewise via \texttt{isBigO\_pi}. For a concrete aRTS design this is fully discharged in
\texttt{AlphaRAR.aRTS\_rho\_rate}: consistency $\hat{\Theta}_n\to\Theta$ is
\texttt{aRTS\_theta\_consistent} (Lemma~\ref{lem:theta_consistent}) and the coordinatewise rate is the
subsampled loglog LIL (Lemma~\ref{lem:theta_LIL}), fed through the positive allocation proportion, so
the only remaining hypotheses are Condition~\textbf{B} (differentiability and non-sparsity) and the
Condition~\textbf{A} moments.

target terms around $v_k$,
$U_{n,k}-U_{\ell_n,k}
 = (n-\ell_n)\big[-(1-\alpha)v_k - (\hat{\rho}_{n,k}-v_k)
   + \frac{\alpha}{n-\ell_n}\sum_{m=\ell_n}^{n-1}(\hat{\rho}_{m,k}-v_k)\big]
   + M_{n,k}-M_{\ell_n,k} + \ell_n(\hat{\rho}_{\ell_n,k}-\hat{\rho}_{n,k})$.
By Theorem~\ref{thm:LLN}, $\hat{\rho}_n\to v$, so both $\hat{\rho}_{n,k}-v_k$ and
the Cesàro average $\frac1{n-\ell_n}\sum_{m=\ell_n}^{n-1}(\hat{\rho}_{m,k}-v_k)$
are $o(1)$ (treating separately the bounded and diverging cases of $\ell_n$).

\texttt{AlphaRAR.auxU\_sub}; the $o(1)$ remainder $\alpha\sum_{[\ell_n,n)}(\hat\rho_m-v)

\texttt{AlphaRAR.abs\_sum\_Ico\_sub\_le\_of\_tendsto} (valid for an arbitrary window, bounded or
diverging) and its second by $\hat\rho_n\to v$.

By Corollary~\ref{cor:mart_Op}, $Q_{n,k}=O_p(\sqrt n)$, hence
$\hat{\theta}_{n,k}-\theta_k = Q_{n,k}/N_{n,k} + o_p(N_{n,k}^{-1/2}) = O_p(n^{-1/2})$
using $N_{n,k}\sim v_k n$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:theta_error_Q}). The Taylor expansion of
$\rho$ gives $\hat{\rho}_n - v = G(\hat{\Theta}_n-\Theta)+O_p(1/n)$ and similarly
at $\ell_n$; subtracting,
$\ell_n(\hat{\rho}_{\ell_n}-\hat{\rho}_n)
 = \ell_n G(\hat{\Theta}_{\ell_n}-\hat{\Theta}_n) + O_p(1)$, so
$|\ell_n(\hat{\rho}_{\ell_n}-\hat{\rho}_n)| \le C\ell_n\|\hat{\Theta}_{\ell_n}-\hat{\Theta}_n\| + O_p(1)$.
Writing the estimator difference through $Q$ (splitting into the increment
$\sum_{j=\ell_n+1}^n$ and the reweighting of $\sum_{j\le\ell_n}$) and bounding
each piece using $N_{n,k}-N_{\ell_n,k}\le n-\ell_n$ and the SLLN, the three
resulting terms are respectively $C\|Q_n-Q_{\ell_n}\|$, $o(1)(n-\ell_n)$ and
$o_p(\sqrt n)$.

$\ell_n|\hat\rho_{\ell_n,k}-\hat\rho_{n,k}| \le V_\rho(n-\ell_n)+W_\rho$ with $V_\rho=o_p(1)$,
$W_\rho=o_p(\sqrt n)$, which is what the drift-sign step consumes. The Condition-\textbf{B} input
enters as the single hypothesis \texttt{hlip} (the target is Lipschitz near $\Theta$, so
$|\hat\rho_{\ell,k}-\hat\rho_{n,k}|\le L\sum_{k'}|\hat\theta_{\ell,k'}-\hat\theta_{n,k'}|$
eventually) --- mirroring how \texttt{clt\_rho} takes the derivative as a hypothesis. The
estimator-increment control $\ell|\hat\theta_{\ell,k'}-\hat\theta_{n,k'}|\le g_{k'}(n-\ell)+h_{k'}
|Q_{n,k'}-Q_{\ell,k'}|$ is \texttt{AlphaRAR.abs\_estimator\_diff\_le}; the coefficients are

therefore enters the $o_p$ bookkeeping through $O_p\cdot o_p=o_p$
(\texttt{IsBigOpOne.mul\_littleOp}). The $Q$-increment control
$|Q_{n,k'}-Q_{\ell,k'}|\le Q_v(n-\ell)+Q_w$ is \texttt{qm\_increments\_resp}.

nodes.name: The regularity hypothesis is necessary
nodes.statement: The weaker hypothesis ``N_n,ktoinfty a.s.'' does not suffice when the index is chosen adaptively. Take one arm with i.i.d.\ mathcal N(theta,V) responses; by the law of the iterated logarithm limsup_m S_m/sqrtVm=+infty a.s., so an algorithm may pull the arm until S_M/sqrtVM>1, then pause it for the next M rounds, and repeat forever. Then N_n,ktoinfty, yet during every pause Q_n,k/sqrtV N_n,k=S_M/sqrtVM>1 is frozen above its typical value on a positive fraction of rounds, so no mathcal N(0,1) limit is possible. This is why the statement is formulated with the regularity N_n,k/c_k,nto1, which is exactly what the Slutsky step consumes.

\label{rem:componentwise_regularity}
The weaker hypothesis ``$N_{n,k}\to\infty$ a.s.'' does \emph{not} suffice when the index is chosen
adaptively. Take one arm with i.i.d.\ $\mathcal N(\theta,V)$ responses; by the law of the iterated
logarithm $\limsup_m S_m/\sqrt{Vm}=+\infty$ a.s., so an algorithm may pull the arm until
$S_M/\sqrt{VM}>1$, then pause it for the next $M$ rounds, and repeat forever. Then

above its typical value on a positive fraction of rounds, so no $\mathcal N(0,1)$ limit is possible.

what the Slutsky step consumes.

Normalize arm $k$ by the \emph{deterministic} $\sqrt{c_{k,n}}$. By the Cramér--Wold device it
suffices to treat a scalar projection $\sum_k w_k Q_{n,k}/\sqrt{c_{k,n}}$; since the arm indicators
are disjoint, this is again a single martingale-difference array (row $n$ has increments
$\sum_k (w_k/\sqrt{c_{k,n}})X_{i,k}(\xi_{i,k}-\theta_k)$), whose predictable variation is
$\sum_k w_k^2 V_k N_{n,k}/c_{k,n}\to\sum_k w_k^2V_k$ by regularity, and which satisfies the
conditional Lindeberg condition since $c_{k,n}\to\infty$. Theorem~\ref{thm:mart_clt} and
Cramér--Wold give $(Q_{n,k}/\sqrt{c_{k,n}})_k\overset{\mathcal{D}}{\longrightarrow}\mathcal N(0,\mathrm{diag}(V_k))$. The
coordinatewise scaling $\sqrt{c_{k,n}/N_{n,k}}\to1$ in probability, so multivariate Slutsky
transfers the limit to the self-normalized vector $(Q_{n,k}/\sqrt{N_{n,k}})_k$. Finally the Bahadur
identity (Lemma~\ref{lem:estimator_bahadur}) and one more Slutsky step give the statement for
$D_n(\hat{\Theta}_n-\Theta)$.

device is that the weighted martingale array \texttt{AlphaRAR.wArray} carries \emph{row-dependent}
weights $w^{(n)}_k = w_k/\sqrt{c_{k,n}}$, so one array covers both a common normalizer and per-arm
ones; the Cramér--Wold projection is
\texttt{AlphaRAR.wLinComb\_scaled\_tendsto\_gaussianReal}. Taking $c_{k,n}=n$ (with
$N_{n,k}/n\to v_k>0$) recovers Corollary~\ref{cor:mart_clt_componentwise}; taking per-arm $c_{k,n}$
with limit $1$ gives the sparse form used in Chapter~\ref{chap:forced}. Note that a linear

(Lemma~\ref{lem:anscombe_clt}) does not jointify; the martingale-array route above does, precisely
because the arm indicators are disjoint.

nodes.name: Scope of the sparse CLT
nodes.statement: The hypothesis that a sparse arm is eventually fed only by forced exploration is a genuine restriction, not an artifact. Since Tge0 and T(Theta)_k=0, the point Theta minimises T_k, so nabla T_k(Theta)=0 and T(hatTheta_n)_k=O(\|hatTheta_n-Theta\|^2). A design that chases its target then allocates arm k about n\,T(hatTheta_n)_kasymp n/N_n,k pulls, i.e.\ N_n,kasympsqrt n --- which dominates h(n)=o(sqrt n). For such designs (e.g.\ the distance-based example, where delta_m,k=(hatrho_m,k-N_m,k/m)^+>0 keeps feeding arm k) forced exploration does not set the scale, and whether N_n,k/sqrt n converges is a delicate question about the feedback between the estimator's own fluctuations and the sampling rate. By Remark~ the conclusion cannot be obtained from N_n,ktoinfty alone, so this case is genuinely open.
nodes.raw_latex:
\label{rem:sparse_clt_scope}
The hypothesis that a sparse arm is eventually fed only by forced exploration is a genuine
restriction, not an artifact. Since $T\ge0$ and $T(\Theta)_k=0$, the point $\Theta$ minimises
$T_k$, so $\nabla T_k(\Theta)=0$ and $T(\hat{\Theta}_n)_k=O(\|\hat{\Theta}_n-\Theta\|^2)$. A design
that \emph{chases} its target then allocates arm $k$ about $n\,T(\hat{\Theta}_n)_k\asymp n/N_{n,k}$
pulls, i.e.\ $N_{n,k}\asymp\sqrt n$ --- which dominates $h(n)=o(\sqrt n)$. For such designs (e.g.\ the
distance-based example, where $\delta_{m,k}=(\hat\rho_{m,k}-N_{m,k}/m)^+>0$ keeps feeding arm $k$)
forced exploration does \emph{not} set the scale, and whether $N_{n,k}/\sqrt n$ converges is a
delicate question about the feedback between the estimator's own fluctuations and the sampling rate.
By Remark~\ref{rem:componentwise_regularity} the conclusion cannot be obtained from
$N_{n,k}\to\infty$ alone, so this case is genuinely open.

nodes.name: Pearson statistic
nodes.statement: Let S_n,k := N_n,khattheta_n,k and tildetheta_n := sum_k=1^K fracN_n,knhattheta_n,k be the pooled estimator. The Pearson chi-square statistic is \[ X_n := sum_k=1^K frac(S_n,k - N_n,ktildetheta_n)^2 N_n,ktildetheta_n(1-tildetheta_n). \]
nodes.raw_latex:
\label{def:pearson_stat}

Let $S_{n,k} := N_{n,k}\hat{\theta}_{n,k}$ and
$\tilde{\theta}_n := \sum_{k=1}^K \frac{N_{n,k}}{n}\hat{\theta}_{n,k}$ be the
pooled estimator. The \emph{Pearson chi-square statistic} is
\[
  \mathcal{X}_n := \sum_{k=1}^K \frac{(S_{n,k} - N_{n,k}\tilde{\theta}_n)^2}
                                        {N_{n,k}\tilde{\theta}_n(1-\tilde{\theta}_n)}.
\]

For a square-integrable martingale $(M_n)$ with $M_0=0$, the transform
\[
  T_n := \sum_{k<n} \frac{\Delta M_k}{1+\langle M\rangle_{k+1}}

$\mathbb{E}[T_n^2] = \sum_{k<n} \mathbb{E}\!\big[\tfrac{\Delta\langle M\rangle_k}{(1+\langle M\rangle_{k+1})^2}\big]

$\tfrac{\Delta\langle M\rangle_k}{(1+\langle M\rangle_{k+1})^2}\le
\tfrac1{1+\langle M\rangle_k}-\tfrac1{1+\langle M\rangle_{k+1}}$.

$O(\sqrt{\langle M\rangle_n\log\langle M\rangle_n})$ upper bound, formalized in

Borel--Cantelli over the blocks (Lemmas~\ref{lem:trunc_block}--\ref{lem:trunc_block_summable})
gives that a.s.\ for all large $k$ and every $m\le 2^k$, $\langle\tilde M\rangle_m\le\sigma^2 2^k
\Rightarrow \tilde M_m<\lambda_k$ (formalized as
\texttt{ae\_eventually\_truncRespMart\_lt\_block}, the summable first Borel--Cantelli step). To
bound a fixed time $n$, take the \emph{least} $k$ with $n\le 2^k$; then $2^k\le 2n$ and
$k\le\log_2 n+1$, and the quadratic-variation bound $\langle\tilde M\rangle_n\le V_k N_{n,k}\le V_k
n\le V_k 2^k$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:trunc_qv_le}) supplies the block hypothesis at $m=n\le 2^k$, giving
$\tilde M_n<\lambda_k=C\sqrt{2^k k}\le C'\sqrt{n\log n}$.

\textbf{Scale.} Because the increment bound $|\Delta\tilde M_i|\le2\sqrt i$ \emph{grows}, the block
horizon $m\le 2^k$ forces the least admissible $k$ to satisfy $2^k\ge n$, so time-blocking delivers
the \emph{time} scale $O(\sqrt{n\log n})$ rather than the variance scale
$O(\sqrt{\langle\tilde M\rangle_n\log\langle\tilde M\rangle_n})=O(\sqrt{N_n\log N_n})$ of the
displayed statement. The two coincide when arm $k$ is sampled a positive fraction of the time
($N_{n,k}\asymp n$, the regime of interest); the sharper variance-scale bound would require blocking
by the quadratic variation rather than by the natural time, and is not formalized. The time-scale
form is exactly parallel to the bounded-increment Corollary~\ref{cor:lil_upper_nat}
(\texttt{ae\_eventually\_le\_sqrt\_nat\_mul\_log}).

\label{lem:llil_qv_stop}

This is the standard device of the martingale LIL \cite{Stout1970,HallHeyde1980} (see also
\cite{Freedman1975} for the underlying exponential inequality): the geometric \emph{block base}
must act on the quadratic variation itself (via a random stopping time), \emph{not} on a
deterministic time horizon. A deterministic-horizon blocking $2^j$ (as in the $O$-rate engine of
Chapter~\ref{chap:pre_lil}) unavoidably loses a factor $\sqrt2$ in the constant when passing to the
$\langle M\rangle_n$ scale, so it yields the $O$-rate but never the sharp constant~$1$; the
sharp constant requires block base $\eta\downarrow1$ on $\langle M\rangle$, which is exactly this
quadratic-variation stopping.
For $v>0$ let $\tau_v:=\inf\{n:\ \langle M\rangle_{n+1}>v\}$. Because $\langle M\rangle$
is predictable ($\langle M\rangle_{n+1}$ is $\mathcal{F}_n$-measurable), $\tau_v$ is a
stopping time, and on $\{n\le\tau_v\}$ one has $\langle M\rangle_n\le v$. The stopped
process $M^{\tau_v}_n:=M_{n\wedge\tau_v}$ is a martingale with
$\langle M^{\tau_v}\rangle_n=\langle M\rangle_{n\wedge\tau_v}$, and under \textbf{(H)}
with constant $A$ its increments obey $|\Delta M^{\tau_v}_i|\le C(v):=A\sqrt{v/\log\log v}$
a.e.\ for all $i$ (for $v$ large), since for $i<\tau_v$ we have $\langle M\rangle_i\le v$
and past $\tau_v$ the increments vanish. Moreover
\[
  \{\exists n:\ M_n\ge\lambda,\ \langle M\rangle_n\le v\}\ \subseteq\
  \{\exists n:\ M^{\tau_v}_n\ge\lambda,\ \langle M^{\tau_v}\rangle_n\le v\}.
\]

\label{lem:llil_refined_freedman}


Under $|\Delta M_i|\le c$ and $|\theta|c\le\eta_\delta$, the process
$Z_n=\exp\!\big(\theta M_n-\tfrac12(1+\delta)\theta^2\langle M\rangle_n\big)$ is a
supermartingale, and hence for $\lambda,v>0$,
\[
  \mathbb{P}\big(\exists n:\ M_n\ge\lambda,\ \langle M\rangle_n\le v\big)\ \le\
  \exp\!\big(-\theta\lambda+\tfrac12(1+\delta)\theta^2 v\big).
\]
Optimizing at $\theta=\lambda/((1+\delta)v)$ (admissible when
$\lambda c\le(1+\delta)v\,\eta_\delta$) gives the bound
$\exp\!\big(-\lambda^2/(2(1+\delta)v)\big)$.

This is the classical Hartman--Wintner
LIL \cite{HartmanWintner1941}: it holds under a bare second moment, and that sharpness
is exactly what makes it delicate. A single truncation at the LIL scale

Borel--Cantelli route of Chapter~\ref{chap:pre_lil} is unavailable.

\label{def:hw_trunc}
Low cutoff $b_j:=\sqrt{j/\log(j+2)}$ (the \emph{log}-level scale, strictly below the LIL
scale $\sqrt{j/L(j)}$) and high cutoff $\sqrt j$. Split each increment into low, medium and
high parts,
\[
  Y_j^{\mathrm L}:=Y_j\mathbf{1}_{\{|Y_j|\le b_j\}},\quad
  Y_j^{\mathrm M}:=Y_j\mathbf{1}_{\{b_j<|Y_j|\le\sqrt j\}},\quad
  Y_j^{\mathrm H}:=Y_j\mathbf{1}_{\{|Y_j|>\sqrt j\}},
\]
so $Y_j=Y_j^{\mathrm L}+Y_j^{\mathrm M}+Y_j^{\mathrm H}$, and set
\[
  \tilde S_m:=\sum_{j\le m}\!\big(Y_j^{\mathrm L}-\mathbb{E} Y_j^{\mathrm L}\big),\quad
  W_m:=\sum_{j\le m}\!\big(Y_j^{\mathrm M}-\mathbb{E} Y_j^{\mathrm M}\big),\quad
  H_m:=\sum_{j\le m}Y_j^{\mathrm H},\quad
  D_m:=\sum_{j\le m}\mathbb{E}\big[Y_j\mathbf{1}_{\{|Y_j|\le\sqrt j\}}\big].
\]
Since $\mathbb{E} Y_j^{\mathrm L}+\mathbb{E} Y_j^{\mathrm M}=\mathbb{E}[Y_j\mathbf{1}_{\{|Y_j|\le\sqrt j\}}]$, one has
$S_m=\tilde S_m+W_m+H_m+D_m$.

$\mathbb{V}\mathrm{ar}(Y_j^{\mathrm M})\le\mathbb{E}[(Y_j^{\mathrm M})^2]=\mathbb{E}[Y^2\mathbf{1}_{\{b_j<|Y|\le\sqrt j\}}]$,
so by Tonelli
\[
  \sum_{j\ge3}\frac{\mathbb{V}\mathrm{ar}(Y_j^{\mathrm M})}{j\,L(j)}\ \le\
  \mathbb{E}\Big[Y^2\!\!\sum_{j:\,b_j<|Y|\le\sqrt j}\frac{1}{j\,L(j)}\Big].
\]
Fix $y=|Y|$. With the log-level cutoff $b_j=\sqrt{j/\log(j+2)}$ the condition
$b_j<y\le\sqrt j$ means $y^2\le j$ and $j/\log(j+2)<y^2$; as $t\mapsto t/\log(t+2)$ is
increasing the latter is $j<j_0(y)$, where $j_0(y)/\log(j_0(y)+2)=y^2$, so
$j_0(y)\asymp y^2\log(y^2)$. Thus $j$ runs over $[y^2,j_0(y))$, an interval of
multiplicative width $\asymp\log(y^2)$ on which $L(j)\asymp L(y^2)$; hence
\[
  \sum_{y^2\le j<j_0(y)}\frac{1}{j\,L(j)}\ \asymp\
  \frac{1}{L(y^2)}\log\frac{j_0(y)}{y^2}\ \asymp\
  \frac{\log\log(y^2)}{L(y^2)}\ =\ O(1),
\]
bounded uniformly in $y$. The inner factor being bounded, the double sum is
$\le C\,\mathbb{E}[Y^2]<\infty$. The mechanism: the medium band is only a $\log$-factor wide, so
the harmonic inner sum is $O(\log\log/\log\log)=O(1)$; this is exactly where the bare
second moment suffices. (The LIL-scale low cutoff $\sqrt{j/L(j)}$ would make the band a
mere $\log\log$-factor wide and the inner sum $\to0$; the log-level cutoff trades that
slack for the sharp-constant condition \textbf{(H)}$\to0$ of the low part, and $O(1)$
still gives convergence.)

\emph{Formalization.} Both the analytic heart and the measure-theoretic wrapper are formalized.
The uniform inner-sum bound $\sum_{j:\,t\le j<t\log(j+2)}1/(j\,L(j))\le C$ (with $t=y^2$) is
\texttt{AlphaRAR.medium\_inner\_tsum\_le}, built from \texttt{AlphaRAR.medium\_sum\_Icc\_big} (the
$t\ge9$ estimate: pull out $1/L(\lceil t\rceil)$ and bound the harmonic sum by
$\log(B/A)\le\log(5\log t)=\log5+L(t)$) via the range bounds \texttt{medium\_crude} ($j<8t^2$) and
\texttt{medium\_tight} ($j<t(\log9+2\log t)$), the harmonic comparison
\texttt{sum\_Icc\_one\_div\_le}, and \texttt{loglog\_le\_loglog}. The wrapper
\texttt{AlphaRAR.medium\_variance\_series\_le} turns it into the second-moment series: by finite-sum
linearity $\sum_{j<n}\big(\int X^2\mathbf{1}_{\{b_j<|X|\le\sqrt j\}}\big)/(j\,L(j))=\int X^2\sum_{j<n}
\mathbf{1}_{\{\dots\}}/(j\,L(j))$, the inner sum is $\le C$ pointwise (at $t=X(\omega)^2$, using
$b_j<|x|\le\sqrt j\iff x^2\le j<x^2\log(j+2)$), so each partial sum is $\le C\,\mathbb{E}[X^2]$ and
$\sum'_j(\dots)\le C\,\mathbb{E}[X^2]$ with the series summable. The reduction
$\mathbb{V}\mathrm{ar}(X\mathbf{1}_{\{b_j<|X|\le\sqrt j\}})\le\mathbb{E}[(X\mathbf{1}_{\{\dots\}})^2]=\mathbb{E}[X^2\mathbf{1}_{\{\dots\}}]$
(\texttt{variance\_le\_expectation\_sq}, $(X\mathbf{1}_S)^2=X^2\mathbf{1}_S$) plus comparison of nonnegative
series (\texttt{Summable.of\_nonneg\_of\_le}) gives \texttt{AlphaRAR.medium\_variance\_summable}:
$\sum_{j\ge3}\mathbb{V}\mathrm{ar}(X\mathbf{1}_{\{b_j<|X|\le\sqrt j\}})/(j\,L(j))<\infty$. Taking $X=Y_0$ and using
$\mathbb{V}\mathrm{ar}(Y_j^{\mathrm M})=\mathbb{V}\mathrm{ar}(Y_0\mathbf{1}_{\{b_j<|Y_0|\le\sqrt j\}})$ (identical distribution) is the
stated series.

Put $a_j:=\sqrt{2\,j\,L(j)}$, positive nondecreasing with $a_j\to\infty$. The partial
sums of the independent, mean-zero terms $(Y_j^{\mathrm M}-\mathbb{E} Y_j^{\mathrm M})/a_{j+1}$
form an $L^2$-bounded martingale, since by independence and Lemma~\ref{lem:hw_medium_var}
\[
  \int\Big(\sum_{j<n}\tfrac{Y_j^{\mathrm M}-\mathbb{E} Y_j^{\mathrm M}}{a_{j+1}}\Big)^2
  =\sum_{j<n}\frac{\mathbb{V}\mathrm{ar}(Y_j^{\mathrm M})}{a_{j+1}^2}
  \le\tfrac12\sum_{j}\frac{\mathbb{V}\mathrm{ar}(Y_j^{\mathrm M})}{j\,L(j)}<\infty .
\]
Hence $\sum_j(Y_j^{\mathrm M}-\mathbb{E} Y_j^{\mathrm M})/a_{j+1}$ converges a.s.\ by the $L^2$
martingale convergence theorem (Lemma~\ref{lem:slln_l2_conv}), and Kronecker's lemma with
weights $b_j=a_j$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:kronecker_general}, whose conclusion
$a_m^{-1}\sum_{j<m}a_{j+1}y_j\to0$ with $y_j=(Y_j^{\mathrm M}-\mathbb{E} Y_j^{\mathrm M})/a_{j+1}$
is exactly $a_m^{-1}\sum_{j<m}(Y_j^{\mathrm M}-\mathbb{E} Y_j^{\mathrm M})\to0$) gives
$W_m=o(a_m)=o(\sqrt{m\,L(m)})$ a.s. This is the Kolmogorov-convergence-plus-Kronecker
pattern of the martingale SLLN (Chapter~\ref{chap:pre_slln}); both ingredients are
already formalized.

By Definition~\ref{def:hw_trunc}, $S_m=\tilde S_m+W_m+H_m+D_m$, and the three remainders
are $o(\sqrt{m\,L(m)})$: $H_m=O(1)$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:hw_high}), $W_m=o(\sqrt{m\,L(m)})$
(Lemma~\ref{lem:hw_medium}) and $D_m=o(\sqrt m)$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:hw_drift}). Hence
$\limsup_m S_m/\sqrt{2\sigma^2 m\,L(m)}=\limsup_m\tilde S_m/\sqrt{2\sigma^2 m\,L(m)}\le1$
by the sharp low-part bound (Lemma~\ref{lem:hw_low_H}). No $A_0\to0$ limit (as in
de~Acosta's LIL-scale truncation) is needed: the log-level cutoff $b_j\to\infty$ already
gives $\mathbb{V}\mathrm{ar}(Y_j^{\mathrm L})\to\sigma^2$, so the constant is sharp. The two-sided statement
applies this to $-Y$.

\emph{Formalization} (\texttt{AlphaRAR.iid\_hartmanWintner\_limsup\_le\_one}). Because Mathlib's
\texttt{truncation} is half-open $(-b_j,b_j]$, the pointwise identity $Y_j=Y_j^{\mathrm L}+
Y_j^{\mathrm M}+Y_j^{\mathrm H}$ fails only at the single boundary atom $\{Y_j=-b_j\}$, where the
uncovered mass is $-b_j\le0$; \emph{dropping} it gives the one-sided pointwise bound $Y_j\le
Y_j^{\mathrm L}+Y_j^{\mathrm M}+Y_j\mathbf{1}_{\{|Y_j|>\sqrt j\}}$ (\texttt{le\_lowMedHigh}), enough for the
upper half. The drift picks up the atom in expectation, controlled by $\sum_j b_j\,\mathbb{P}(Y_j=-b_j)\le
\mathbb{E}|Y_0|<\infty$ (\texttt{sum\_atom\_le}, using that the distinct $-b_j$ index disjoint events).
A coboundedness-free core (\texttt{hw\_eventually}) proves ``a.s.\ $\forall\beta>1$ eventually
$S_m\le\beta\sqrt{2\sigma^2 m\,L(m)}$''; applying it to $-Y$ gives the matching lower bound
$S_m\ge-\beta\sqrt{2\sigma^2 m\,L(m)}$, which supplies the coboundedness needed to pass to the
$\limsup$. The nondegeneracy $\sigma^2>0$ is used so the weight is eventually positive.

\label{lem:opt_skip}

Consider an algorithm--environment sequence $(A_j,Y_j)_{j\ge0}$ in a stationary environment with
per-arm reward kernel $\nu$: the response $Y_j$ is drawn from $\nu(A_j)$, independent of the history
given the current arm (the action-augmented filtration $\mathcal{F}_{j-1}\vee\sigma(A_j)$). Fix an arm $k$
pulled infinitely often a.s., and let $\tau_0<\tau_1<\cdots$ enumerate the pulls $\{j:A_j=k\}$. Then
the sampled responses $(Y_{\tau_m})_{m\ge0}$ are i.i.d.\ with law $\nu_k$.

nodes.statement: The classical optional-skipping argument, with the selector D_j=1_\A_j=k\. Decompose over the value j of the m-th pull time tau_m: the event \tau_m=j\ coincides a.s.\ with the predictable hit event \N_j=m,\ A_j=k\ (where N_j=\#\i<j:A_i=k\), which is measurable for the action-augmented sigma-algebra at time j, and on it the conditional law of Y_j is the constant nu_k (condExp\_feedback). Hence, for any prefix and measurable sets E_i, P\!big(bigcap_i<NY_tau_i^-1E_ibig)=prod_i<Nnu_k(E_i) by induction on N, peeling the newest sample and summing over its a.s.-covering, pairwise-disjoint pull events; this is independence together with each marginal =nu_k. Formalization. The combinatorial core is generic (AlphaRAR.iIndepFun\_sampledSeq, map\_sampledSeq\_eq): for a predictable \0,1\-selector D and a process Y whose value is rho-fresh given the current sigma-algebra on \D_j=1\ (hfact: mu(Y_j^-1Ecap S)=rho(E)\,mu(S) for Ssubseteq\D_j=1\), the samples at the hit times of D are i.i.d.\ rho. The hit time tau_m is Nat.nth, and the honestly sigma-algebra-measurable hit events replace the (absent from Mathlib) random stopping-time sigma-algebra. The freshness hfact is discharged for the response process (hfact\_stationaryEnv) from the stationary-environment conditional distribution. This general statement is not yet in Mathlib and is a worthwhile contribution.

nodes.raw_latex:
\label{lem:clt_truncation}

Fix a constant $B$ with $\sigma^2<B$ (e.g.\ $B:=\sigma^2+1$). Define the stopped
array by truncating increment $i$ as soon as the \emph{next} partial variance
would exceed $B$:
\[
  \bar\Delta_{n,i}:=\Delta_{n,i}\,\mathbf{1}_{\{V_{n,i+1}\le B\}},
  \qquad V_{n,i+1}=\textstyle\sum_{l\le i}v_{n,l}.
\]
The indicator is $\mathcal{F}_i$-measurable, since $V_{n,i+1}$ depends only on
$v_{n,0},\dots,v_{n,i}$, all $\mathcal{F}_i$-measurable. Then:
\begin{enumerate}
  \item[(i)] $\bar\Delta_{n,i}$ is again a martingale difference array for
        $(\mathcal{F}_i)$, with per-step variances
        $\bar v_{n,i}=v_{n,i}\mathbf{1}_{\{V_{n,i+1}\le B\}}$;
  \item[(ii)] its predictable variation is bounded \emph{by the constant $B$}:
        $\bar V_n=\sum_{i<k_n}\bar v_{n,i}\le B$ everywhere;
  \item[(iii)] $\bar V_n\xrightarrow{\mathbb{P}}\sigma^2$, and $\bar\Delta_{n,i}$
        satisfies the conditional Lindeberg condition;
  \item[(iv)] $P\big(\bar S_n\ne S_n\big)\le P(V_n>B)\to0$, where
        $\bar S_n=\sum_{i<k_n}\bar\Delta_{n,i}$.
\end{enumerate}
Consequently $S_n$ and $\bar S_n$ have the same characteristic-function limit, and
it suffices to prove the theorem under the extra assumption $V_n\le B$ a.s.

The one-step increment factorises as
$Z_{n,j+1}-Z_{n,j}=Z_{n,j}\big(\exp(it\Delta_{n,j}+\tfrac{t^2}{2}v_{n,j})-1\big)$,
where the factor $Z_{n,j}$ is $\mathcal{F}_j$-measurable. Taking conditional
expectation and using Lemma~\ref{lem:clt_cond_char},
\[
  \mathbb{E}[Z_{n,j+1}-Z_{n,j}\mid\mathcal{F}_j]
  = Z_{n,j}\Big(e^{(t^2/2)v_{n,j}}\big(1-\tfrac{t^2}{2}v_{n,j}+r_{n,j}\big)-1\Big).
\]
Writing $y=\tfrac{t^2}{2}v_{n,j}\ (\le\tfrac{t^2}{2}B')$, the bracket splits as
$\big(e^{y}(1-y)-1\big)+e^{y}r_{n,j}$; by
Lemma~\ref{lem:clt_real_exp_bound_pos}, $|e^{y}(1-y)-1|\le y^2 e^{y}
=\tfrac{t^4}{4}v_{n,j}^2\,e^{y}$. Hence the modulus is
$\le|Z_{n,j}|\,e^{(t^2/2)B'}\big(\tfrac{t^4}{4}v_{n,j}^2+\|r_{n,j}\|\big)$.
(The unbounded form of the elementary bound is essential here: $y$ is only bounded,
not $\le1$.) Summing over $j$, telescoping and using the tower property
$\mathbb{E}[Z_{n,k_n}-Z_{n,0}]=\sum_j\mathbb{E}\big[\mathbb{E}[Z_{n,j+1}-Z_{n,j}\mid\mathcal{F}_j]\big]$,
\[
  \big|\mathbb{E}[Z_{n,k_n}]-1\big|
  \le e^{(t^2/2)B'}\,\mathbb{E}\!\Big[\tfrac{t^4}{4}\textstyle\sum_j v_{n,j}^2
      + e^{(t^2/2)B'}\sum_j\|r_{n,j}\|\Big].
\]
Both sums tend to $0$ in probability
(Lemmas~\ref{lem:clt_sum_var_sq},~\ref{lem:clt_sum_rem}) and are uniformly
bounded, so by bounded convergence the expectations tend to $0$.

\label{thm:mart_clt}


Let $(\Delta_{n,i})_{i<k_n}$ be a martingale difference array (as in the standing
setup) with predictable quadratic variation $V_n\xrightarrow{\mathbb{P}}\sigma^2$ and
satisfying the conditional Lindeberg condition
$L_n(\varepsilon)\xrightarrow{\mathbb{P}}0$ for every $\varepsilon>0$. Then the row sums
converge in distribution,
\[
  S_n=\sum_{i<k_n}\Delta_{n,i} \;\overset{\mathcal{D}}{\longrightarrow}\; \mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^2).
\]
In Lean the conclusion has the shape of Mathlib's i.i.d.\ central limit theorem: for every random
variable $Y$ (on any probability space) with law $\mathcal N(0,\sigma^2)$, $S_n$ converges to $Y$
in distribution (\texttt{TendstoInDistribution}); the convergence of the laws of $S_n$ themselves
is the case $Y=\mathrm{id}$ on $(\mathbb{R},\mathcal N(0,\sigma^2))$.

Then the row sums converge in distribution, \[ S_n=sum_i<k_nDelta_n,i \;oversetDlongrightarrow\; N(0,sigma^2). \] In Lean the conclusion has the shape of Mathlib's i.i.d.\ central limit theorem: for every random variable Y (on any probability space) with law mathcal N(0,sigma^2), S_n converges to Y in distribution (TendstoInDistribution); the convergence of the laws of S_n themselves is the case Y=id on (R,mathcal N(0,sigma^2)).

\[

Normalize $Q_{n,k}$ by the \emph{deterministic} $\sqrt{V_k v_k n}$: the increments
$\Delta_{m}=X_{m,k}(\xi_{m,k}-\theta_k)/\sqrt{V_k v_k n}$ form a martingale-difference array (for the
action-augmented filtration) whose predictable variation is $N_{n,k}/(v_k n)\xrightarrow{\mathbb{P}}1$
(consistency) and which satisfies the conditional Lindeberg condition, because the sampled responses
are i.i.d.\ with finite variance $V_k$ (each cell contributes
$\mathbf{1}\{A_m=k\}\,V_k^{-1}v_k^{-1}n^{-1}\mathbb{E}[(\xi-\theta_k)^2\mathbf{1}\{|\xi-\theta_k|>\varepsilon\sqrt{V_k v_k n}\}]$
and the truncated moment vanishes by dominated convergence). Theorem~\ref{thm:mart_clt} then gives
$Q_{n,k}/\sqrt{V_k v_k n}\overset{\mathcal{D}}{\longrightarrow}\mathcal N(0,1)$. Finally
$\sqrt{V_k v_k n}/\sqrt{V_k N_{n,k}}=\sqrt{v_k n/N_{n,k}}\xrightarrow{\mathbb{P}}1$, so Slutsky yields the
stated random-normalizer limit.

By the Cramér--Wold device it suffices to prove that every scalar projection converges: for each
$w\in\mathbb{R}^K$, $\langle w, Q_n/\sqrt n\rangle = \big(\sum_k w_k Q_{n,k}\big)/\sqrt n$. The increments
$\sum_k w_k X_{i,k}(\xi_{i,k}-\theta_k)$ form a single martingale-difference array (the arm indicators
are disjoint, so the conditional square is $\sum_k w_k^2\mathbf{1}\{A_i=k\}V_k$, giving predictable
variation $\sum_k w_k^2 V_k N_{n,k}/n\to\sum_k w_k^2 v_kV_k$; the conditional Lindeberg condition
holds arm-by-arm by dominated convergence). Theorem~\ref{thm:mart_clt} yields
$\big(\sum_k w_k Q_{n,k}\big)/\sqrt n\overset{\mathcal{D}}{\longrightarrow}\mathcal N(0,\sum_k w_k^2 v_kV_k)$, which is precisely the
projection $\langle w,\cdot\rangle$ of the diagonal Gaussian (whose covariance is
$\mathrm{diag}(v_kV_k)$ by orthogonality of the coordinates, Lemma~\ref{lem:qv_orthogonal}). Cramér--Wold
then gives the joint limit.

By the exact Bahadur identity (Lemma~\ref{lem:estimator_bahadur}),
$\hat\theta_{n,k}-\theta_k=(Q_{n,k}+(\theta_{0,k}-\theta_k))/(N_{n,k}+1)$, so
\[
  \sqrt{N_{n,k}}(\hat\theta_{n,k}-\theta_k)
    = \frac{Q_{n,k}}{\sqrt{N_{n,k}}}\cdot\frac{N_{n,k}}{N_{n,k}+1}
      + (\theta_{0,k}-\theta_k)\frac{\sqrt{N_{n,k}}}{N_{n,k}+1}.
\]
The self-normalized martingale vector $(Q_{n,k}/\sqrt{N_{n,k}})_k$ converges jointly to
$\mathcal N(0,\mathrm{diag}(V_k))$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:mart_clt_joint_selfnorm}), while the two
coordinatewise scaling factors tend to $1$ and $0$ in probability (as $N_{n,k}\to\infty$).
Multivariate Slutsky (a continuous coordinatewise affine map against the constant limit $(1,0)$)

  \;\overset{\mathcal{D}}{\longrightarrow}\; \mathcal N(0,v).
\]

claim.
